title: Number systems: binary, hex, two’s complement

layers.basics: Computers use binary (0/1); hexadecimal is shorthand grouping four bits. Two’s complement represents negative numbers so addition works the same.
layers.deeper: An n-bit two’s-complement word spans −2ⁿ⁻¹…2ⁿ⁻¹−1; overflow is detected when carry into and out of the top bit differ.
layers.expert: Other encodings include BCD (one decimal digit per four bits), Gray code (adjacent values differ in one bit), fixed-point Qm.n, and IEEE-754 floating point (sign, exponent, mantissa).

layers.basics: Rules like A+AB=A and De Morgan’s laws shrink a logic expression and thus the circuit.
layers.deeper: Sum-of-products and product-of-sums forms; any function is built from AND/OR/NOT.
layers.expert: Shannon expansion f=x f_x+x′f_x′; consensus theorem; duality; minimal forms are NP-hard in general.

title: Logic gates
summary: AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR, XOR.

layers.basics: Gates are the atoms of digital logic. NAND and NOR are universal: any logic can be built from either.
layers.deeper: Truth tables define behaviour; gate symbols (ANSI/IEEE); fan-in and fan-out limit practical use.
layers.expert: Propagation delay, noise margin V_IL/V_IH/V_OL/V_OH, logic families (TTL, CMOS, ECL); tristate and open-drain outputs for buses.

layers.basics: A K-map arranges a truth table so neighbours differ by one bit; circle groups of 1s to get simple terms.
layers.deeper: Practical for up to 4 variables (5 or 6 with stacked maps); rows and columns are in Gray-code order so adjacent cells differ in one variable; don’t-cares enlarge groups; watch for hazards.
layers.expert: Prime implicants and essential prime implicants; static-1 hazards removed by redundant terms.

layers.basics: A tabular algorithm that finds an exact minimal two-level (sum-of-products) form of a Boolean function. It is guaranteed correct but too slow for large functions, so synthesis tools use heuristics such as Espresso.
layers.deeper: Step 1 merges terms that differ in exactly one bit, round after round, until only prime implicants remain. Step 2 chooses the fewest primes that cover every minterm, starting with the essential ones; this is a set-cover problem and NP-hard.
layers.expert: Complexity grows exponentially; Espresso heuristic and BDDs are used in practice; ABC for multi-level.

layers.basics: A multiplexer chooses one of many inputs; a decoder turns a binary code into one active line; an encoder does the reverse.
layers.deeper: A 2ⁿ:1 mux is a universal logic element; memories use decoders for addresses.
layers.expert: Mux-based function realisation (Shannon); priority encoders; one-hot vs binary encoding.

layers.basics: A half adder adds two bits; a full adder includes carry in. Chain them for multi-bit addition.
layers.deeper: Ripple-carry is simple but slow; hierarchical carry-lookahead and parallel-prefix adders (such as Kogge–Stone) reduce delay from O(n) to O(log n) gate levels, at the cost of more area and wiring.
layers.expert: Sum=A⊕B⊕C, Cout=AB+C(A⊕B); Kogge–Stone prefix adder; subtraction via two’s complement; multipliers (array, Booth, Wallace).

title: Arithmetic logic unit (ALU)
summary: The calculator at the heart of a CPU.

layers.basics: An ALU performs add, subtract, AND, OR, shifts and compares on binary words, selected by control bits.
layers.deeper: Flags (zero, carry, overflow, negative) report results for branching.
layers.expert: Bit-slice design with mux per bit; barrel shifters; overflow V=C_in⊕C_out for two’s complement.

layers.basics: Two cross-coupled gates hold a bit; that is an SR latch. A gated D-latch stores whatever D was while enabled.
layers.deeper: Level sensitivity makes them tricky in clocked systems; used in clock gating and some high-speed design.
layers.expert: Metastability when S and R de-assert together; transparent latch timing, time-borrowing.

layers.basics: A flip-flop samples its input on a clock edge and holds the value until the next edge.
layers.deeper: D stores data; T toggles; JK is a generalised version. Two latches back-to-back (master–slave) make an edge-triggered D FF.
layers.expert: Setup/hold constraints; clock-to-Q delay; metastability MTBF=e^{t_r/τ}/(T₀ f_c f_d).

layers.basics: A register stores a multi-bit word; a counter steps through binary values with each clock.
layers.deeper: Shift registers move bits sideways (serial/parallel conversion); synchronous counters avoid ripple delays.
layers.expert: LFSR counters give pseudo-random sequences for test and CDMA; Johnson and Gray counters limit glitches.

layers.basics: An FSM has a finite set of states and rules for moving between them based on inputs. Moore outputs depend on state only; Mealy on state and input.
layers.deeper: Design: state diagram → state table → encode → next-state and output logic.
layers.expert: State encoding (binary, one-hot, Gray) trades area and speed; unreachable states and safe recovery; FSMs written in HDL with case statements.

title: Timing: setup, hold and clocking
summary: Making sure signals arrive in time.

layers.basics: A signal must be stable for a short time before (setup) and after (hold) the clock edge; the slowest path sets the maximum clock.
layers.deeper: For a launch flip-flop feeding a capture flip-flop on one clock, the slowest path must satisfy T_clk ≥ t_cq,max + t_logic,max + t_setup + t_skew + t_jitter, where skew is the adverse case (capture clock early). Hold needs t_cq,min + t_logic,min ≥ t_hold + t_skew. Hold violations are fixed by adding delay, not by slowing the clock.
layers.expert: Static timing analysis, clock domain crossing (two-flop synchroniser), clock trees, jitter, on-chip variation; PVT corners.

formula: T_clk ≥ t_cq,max + t_logic,max + t_setup + t_skew + t_jitter

layers.basics: ROM keeps data without power; SRAM typically uses six transistors per bit and is fast; DRAM uses one transistor plus a capacitor, is dense but needs refreshing.
layers.deeper: Address decoders select rows/columns; sense amplifiers read tiny charges.
layers.expert: SRAM 6T cell stability (SNM); Modern commodity DRAM cells are about 6F² (F is the minimum feature size; older layouts used 8F²). The refresh window was 64 ms for DDR3 and DDR4. For DDR5 it is 32 ms at or below 85 °C and shorter when hotter. JEDEC DDR5 speed grades run from about 4.0 to 8.8 GT/s per pin.

layers.basics: Flash stores bits as charge trapped in a floating gate or charge-trap layer in a transistor; it remains without power.
layers.deeper: NAND flash is written and erased by Fowler–Nordheim tunnelling through a thin oxide, and repeated tunnelling gradually damages that oxide. NOR flash usually programs by hot-electron injection and erases by tunnelling. Modern NAND is stacked in many vertical layers.
layers.expert: SLC/MLC/TLC/QLC store 1–4 bits per cell using 2ⁿ threshold levels; rated program/erase endurance falls as more bits are stored per cell, and it depends on vendor and process; wear levelling and ECC in controllers.

layers.basics: An FPGA contains many small lookup tables and flip-flops joined by programmable wiring; you configure it to be any digital circuit.
layers.deeper: CPLDs are smaller, simpler and typically built on non-volatile flash; FPGAs add block RAM, DSP slices and transceivers.
layers.expert: LUT-4/6 implements any function of its inputs; most FPGAs hold their configuration in SRAM cells loaded from a bitstream at power-up (flash-based and antifuse FPGAs also exist); place-and-route, timing closure.

layers.basics: Write RTL in Verilog/VHDL, simulate it, synthesize it to gates, place and route, then program the chip.
layers.deeper: Synthesis infers registers and combinational logic from the RTL and maps it onto the device’s LUTs and flip-flops. Place-and-route then checks the result against constraints (clock periods, pin locations, I/O standards). Testbenches and waveforms verify the design before hardware.
layers.expert: Synthesis → mapping → P&R → bitstream; timing closure iterations; formal verification and coverage-driven testbenches for ASICs.
